title: The Lesson I Learned From Gideon’s Insecurity
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Gideon’s Insecurity
When God Calls You Mighty but You Only See Your Weakness
There are moments in life when the loudest voice you hear is not the voice of your critics.
The voice that reminds you of your failures.
The voice that replays your mistakes.
The voice that whispers that everyone else is more qualified, more gifted, more spiritual, more successful, more worthy than you.
The voice that says, “Who do you think you are?”
Maybe that voice has followed you for years.
Maybe it followed you into your marriage.
Into every dream God ever placed inside your heart.
If so, then Gideon’s story is not just ancient history.

Because buried within the pages of Judges is one of the most relatable accounts in all of Scripture—a story that begins with insecurity, fear, self-doubt, and hidden shame but ends with God proving that His strength is greater than our weakness.
The lesson I learned from Gideon’s insecurity changed the way I see myself forever.
And maybe it will change the way you see yourself too.

The story begins in Judges 6 during one of Israel’s darkest seasons. The nation had turned away from God, and as a result, the Midianites oppressed them severely. Crops were stolen. Livestock was taken. Families lived in fear.
Many people today are not hiding in caves from Midianites, but they are hiding emotionally.
Because insecurity has a way of making people disappear even when everyone can still see them.
Judges 6:11 tells us Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress.
A winepress was not designed for threshing wheat.
The Hebrew text paints the picture of a man trying not to be noticed.
Trying not to lose what little he had left.
The Angel of the LORD appears and says:
"The LORD is with you, mighty warrior."
God called a hiding man a mighty warrior.
God saw what Gideon could not see.
And that may be the most important lesson of all.
God's calling is not based on your current condition.
It is based on His purpose.
We often introduce ourselves by our wounds.
God introduces us by our destiny.
God saw the future He was writing.
The same thing happens throughout Scripture.
A criminal on a cross becomes a citizen of paradise.
His response reveals the true depth of his insecurity.
"Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."
It convinces us that our limitations are stronger than God's promises.
Instead of saying, "I struggle with fear," we begin saying, "I am fearful."
Instead of saying, "I failed," we begin saying, "I am a failure."
Instead of saying, "I sinned," we begin saying, "I am beyond redemption."
Because if he can make you identify with your weakness, you may never walk in your calling.
Yet God answers Gideon's insecurity with only five words:
The calling was never about Gideon's abilities.
God said, "I will be with you."
God said, "I will be with you."
When the disciples were sent into the world.
"ἐγὼ μεθ’ ὑμῶν εἰμι πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας"
"Ego meth' humōn eimi pasas tas hēmeras."
God never promises that we are enough.
Because Christianity is not confidence in self.
The Gospel says, "His strength is made perfect in weakness."
The Greek word Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 12:9 for weakness is "ἀσθένεια" (astheneia), meaning frailty, inability, or lack of strength.
God does not merely tolerate weakness.
He often chooses it as the stage upon which His power is displayed.
That is exactly what happened with Gideon.
God intentionally reduced Gideon's army from 32,000 soldiers to only 300 men.
Because God wanted everyone to know who deserved the glory.
The victory would not belong to Gideon.
How many of us spend our lives asking God for more strength when He may be asking for more surrender?
How many of us think our greatest obstacle is weakness when our greatest obstacle may actually be self-reliance?
Gideon's insecurity became the very place where God displayed His glory.
And perhaps your weakness can become the same.
Maybe you feel disqualified because of your past.
The cross itself is the greatest example of God transforming apparent weakness into eternal victory.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not for people who have everything together.
Not for people who never struggle.
Not for people who never doubt.
Maybe that is why this story grips me so deeply.
Because I have discovered that insecurity does not disappear by staring at myself longer.
It disappears when I look at Christ longer.
The more Gideon focused on himself, the smaller he became.
The more he trusted God, the stronger he became.
And because of Jesus Christ, grace always has the final word.
Your testimony may encourage someone reading these words who feels completely alone.
Because someone who feels hidden today may discover through your share that God still calls ordinary people into extraordinary purposes.
And perhaps the person God wants to rescue from insecurity next is closer than you think.
The God who found Gideon in a winepress is still finding people in their hiding places today.
